stories.summary: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant is to fly back to Belfast this evening to reconvene talks in an attempt to break the Drumcree parade deadlock. The Orange Order and residents of the Garvaghy Road will be invited to another round of talks as efforts continue to resolve the stand-off. It is expected they could start some time around 7pm. Senior DUP politicians last night said the proposal was unacceptable.

stories.title: Cost of policing Drumcree stand-off at £3m so far - PSNI
stories.summary: The cost of policing the Drumcree stand-off has so far cost £3 million, PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has said. Mr Boutcher has been speaking publicly for the first time in the five-day stand-off, addressing a public session of the Northern Ireland Policing Board this morning. He said the police objective was to facilitate the Parades Commission determination that had approved the parade of 35 Orangemen along the Garvaghy Road. "Without that determination such a parade would be unlawful. What it does not mean is that the police must accommodate that determination at all costs," he said. Mr Boutcher said he also had a statutory responsibility to preserve the peace and maintain order. "We are not back in 1997. We are not expected to, nor will we, force members of the Orange Order, many of whom are of a certain age, through a hostile crowd which will be unsafe and will be disproportionate and where the wider consequences for Northern Ireland could be catastrophic."

stories.title: Irish players 'exposed, hung out to dry' by FAI - Ennis
stories.summary: Social Democrats TD and Spokesperson on Sport Daniel Ennis has said the Ireland players "have been hung out to dry" by the FAI and the board of the association should resign. The FAI is to tell the Oireachtas Sports Committee today how the decision to proceed with the controversial fixtures against Israel was made in the best interests of Irish football. The CEO of the FAI David Courell and other senior figures at the Association will answer questions from TDs and Senators this afternoon with Ireland to play Israel again on Sunday in the UEFA Nations League after preparations for last weekend's fixture in Hungary were thrown into chaos at the eleventh hour. He said it is the biggest crisis facing Irish football, with many people telling him that they will not renew season tickets. Mr Ennis said that the FAI has put "a dark stain" on Irish football. In relation to possible sanctions that the FAI may have faced for not playing the match, Mr Ennis said that "no sanction stands up against the charred remains of babies."

stories.title: September new electric car registrations soar 80% - SIMI
stories.summary: New figures from the Society of the Irish Motor Industry show an 80% jump in the number of new electric cars registered in September compared to the same time last year. The new SIMI figures show that 3,126 new electric cars (battery electric cars) were registered last month, compared to the 1,734 registrations in September of last year. So far this year, 35,195 new electric cars have been registered, marking a 57.3% increase compared to the same time in 2025, when 22,376 electric cars were registered. Today's figures show that overall new car registrations for September were up 13.1% to 6,342 compared to 5,607 the same time last year. Registrations so far this year are up 5.4% to 128,288 from 121,675 on the same time in 2025. Meanwhile, imported used cars saw an 18.9% increase in September to 8,326, compared to 7,000 the same month last year. Year to date imports are up 34.4% to 72,140 from 53,661 in 2025. In the new car market share by engine type, battery electric cars lead the market with a share of 27.43%, followed by hybrid (petrol electric) at 23.68%, petrol at 19.59%, plug-in hybrid at 14.93%, and diesel at 12.36%.

stories.title: Pilot tried to crash Tel Aviv-bound plane - Netanyahu
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the co-pilot of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv tried to crash the plane after stabbing the pilot, but passengers then held him down while other pilots landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia. Describing the event as "a highly severe security incident," Mr Netanyahu said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 from the United Arab Emirates to Israel. The alleged assailant, who an Israeli official identified as an Omani national, was arrested after the plane landed, Mr Netanyahu said. "All passengers are out of harm's way," Mr Netanyahu, who described the passengers as being almost all Israeli, said in a video statement released by his office. The Israeli leader quoted a passenger as saying that passengers along with a member of the crew broke into the cockpit after the aircraft "entered a tailspin and began to dive" and found the co-pilot "trying to sabotage the plane's systems". "They saved many lives. They prevented a heavy disaster," he said.

stories.title: Ireland make six changes for Japan rematch
stories.summary: Jane Clohessy and Niamh Gallagher will both make their first starts for Ireland, while Scott Bemand is set to hand three players their debuts in Saturday's rematch with Japan in Cork. The Ireland head coach has made six changes to the group that defeated Japan 31-24 in Galway on Sunday, with prop Sophie Barrett, lock Kate Jordan and versatile back Alana McInerney all in line for debuts. Aoife Wafer misses out once again due to injury, but captain Erin King, Brittany Hogan and Jemima Adams Verling continue in the back row - the only line of the starting XV that is retained in its entirety from last week. Linda Djougang comes back into the side this week, but is named at loosehead prop where she replaces Niamh O'Dowd, joining Neve Jones and Eilís Cahill in a powerful front row unit. Clohessy, daughter of former Ireland men's international Peter, is named at second row for her third cap and first start, joining Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan at lock, while Dorothy Wall misses out due to a knock. Emily Lane swaps back in for Aoibheann Reilly at scrum-half, partnering with Dannah O'Brien in the half-backs.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice leading candidate to succeed Joyce in Galway
stories.summary: Éamonn Fitzmaurice is in advanced talks with the Galway County Board to take over the manager's position vacated by Pádraic Joyce in early September. It is understood the Finuge clubman has engaged positively with Galway chairman Paul Bellew in recent weeks and is the leading candidate to take charge of the Tribesmen's senior footballers. A three-time All-Ireland winner as a player, Fitzmaurice managed Kerry for six years between 2013 and 2018, leading the Kingdom to Sam Maguire glory in 2014. He also claimed six straight Munster SFC titles and an Allianz League title during his time in charge. He remained involved with the club scene in his native Kerry, coaching the Clifford brothers' club Fossa in 2022 as they claimed a junior All-Ireland title. He was one of the most prominent members of the Football Review Committee, which introduced, trialled and refined the new playing rules that many see as having a revitalising effect on the game since their introduction in 2015.

stories.title: Confirmation Noonan to join Forest at the start of 2027
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers' striker Michael Noonan's departure for Nottingham Forest at the beginning of next year has been confirmed. Nottingham Forest confirmed that the 18-year-old attacker had signed a pre-agreement with the club will be joining the Premier League side in January. Shamrock Rovers posted that Noonan would be leaving at the end of the 2026 League of Ireland season but remains a Hoops player until then and "will play his part in the title run-in over the coming months". Noonan will be out of contract with Shamrock Rovers at the end of the season. The Hoops will receive €180,000 in compensation following the move, as will the striker's previous club, St Patrick's Athletic. Nottingham Forest Chief Football Officer, George Syrianos, said: "Michael is a player we, along with a number of other clubs, have followed closely for some time, so we're delighted he has chosen Nottingham Forest." Noonan, a Republic of Ireland Under-21 international, scored 17 goals in two seasons in Tallaght Stadium and was part of the 2025 double-winning side.

stories.title: Payne embedding a 'strike to score' mentality at Munster
stories.summary: Like every coach, Jared Payne has his own philosophy in how he sees the game. "Play fast. Strike to score quickly. Play smart." It all sounds pretty simple, but having a philosophy and implementing one at the top level is a whole other ball game. Payne made the move back to Ireland over the summer, having spent time with Clermont and the Scarlets following his departure from Ulster back in 2022. His new role sees him in tandem with fellow attack coach Mossy Lawler, as they work together to try and break down opposing defences. The task at hand was bound to be steep, succeeding Mike Prendergast who helped Munster to URC glory in 2023, and who had been widely viewed as a potential future head coach at the province. On the field, the Kiwi works on phases one to three, or your traditional striking phases; with Lawler taking the general phase play which follows. It is a setup which mirrors what Ireland have with Andy Farrell and Andrew Goodman, as the dual-coach role becomes more normal in the modern game. When asked for what he wants from his side, he laid all of his cards on the table speaking to the media on Tuesday. "Play fast. Strike to score quickly. Play smart," he outlined as his core principles.

stories.title: Adventures in audio - The Lyric Feature returns for a new season
stories.summary: But what is The Lyric Feature? It's a place where creative audio makers use the full range of the audible spectrum to tell stories that tickle your brain. It’s a place that regards Irish culture and traditions as something fluid and living, as an inexhaustible source of stories that can be told and retold. It’s a place where unexpected questions are asked and unexpected answers are offered. Here’s some of what’s in store for the Autumn series: What was the first collection of poems written by a black poet published in Ireland? What was it like to be a free-spirited girl in Holy Catholic Ireland in the 1930s and 40s? How did the Irish harp break free from the confines of the parlour to become an instrument integral to traditional music sessions in your local pub? And what kind of music do you get when you pair an Irish hand drum master with a Congelese guitar player? The Jamaican poet Ferdinand Levy arrived in Dublin in the 1940s to study medicine at Trinity College. He brought with him the rhythms and language of the Harlem renaissance and a sensibility shaped by racism and colonialism but also a fresh pair of eyes to the grey streets of Dublin and a playful of the possibilities offered by his new home. In Flashes from the Dark (11th of October) Emma Dabiri tells the story of his contribution to Irish literature. In the same era another poet, Eithne Strong was also making a break for Dublin. The County Limerick writer fled her home at the age of 19, married an Englishman and settled for a time in Dun Laoghaire’s nascent psychoanalytic community. In In the Deeps, Joanna Marsden goes on the trail of a neglected writer who, seeking a freer life, questioned social norms and dared to write from the edges of Irish society. Another unlikely journey is explored by harpist Niamh O’ Brien in From Parlour to Pub (Oct 18th) where she traces the evolution of the Irish harp from the Anglo Irish drawing room to the session in your local pub and in doing so she tells the story of how what seems like a fixed symbol of Irish culture is actually the opposite. The following week, in Dancing to a Different Drum we hear a parallel story of how new instruments are arriving into contemporary Irish music when we meet musician Éamonn Cagney whose immersion in the Irish tradition is complemented by his studies of hand-drums such as the Djembe, the Conga, the Hand-Pan and the Shaker in Ghana and Australia. We’ll hear how Éamonn’s outward looking take on our tradition has led to collaborations which reimagine Irish music such as his work with the Congolese born Irish guitarist Niwel Tsumbu.
stories.rssSummary: RTÉ lyric fm's award winning arts and culture documentary series The Lyric Feature (Sundays 6 pm on RTÉ lyric fm and on RTÉ Listen) returns on October 4th with more engaging stories of our past, present and future.

Limerick playing against Laura Collins of Scartaglen, Co. Kerry. Regan will explain the difference between "a gob****e and an eejit", share his experiences of being an Irishman abroad, and reveal why the Irish accent is a superpower overseas. stories.title: This is why spider season has started early this year
stories.summary: Cosy season is well and truly here, with the chillier weather and blustery showers encouraging us to swap the t-shirts and shorts of summer for the comfort of our sofas. And we're not the only ones taking shelter from the elements indoors: the spiders are at it, too. Our eight-legged friends have reached their mating season, which leads them to move indoors, taking up residence in nooks, crannies, presses and more around the home. "Spider season is fantastic", claims Collie Ennis, a possibly deeply unpopular opinion but one entirely fitting the Biodiversity Officer and Zoology research associate at Trinity College Dublin. "They're all big and bold and they’re out and about, and it’s quite exciting if you’re a bit of a spider nerd", he added, speaking like a spider nerd. By way of explaining this influx of arachnids, Ennis says that this season comes after they’re spent the summer maturing and waiting to breed. "It’s been a good summer for bugs, with the heat and the humidity", he adds. "So they’ve kind of gotten big and bold very fast."

stories.title: UAE, Israel vow to investigate 'root' of plane attack
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel will get to the "root" of the co-pilot who engaged ⁠in a foiled attempt to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight and that Israel will "possibly" be participating in the probe into the incident. Disaster was averted on yesterday's flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was carrying 170 passengers, after the wounded captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker and a reserve crew that had been on board to land the plane in Saudi Arabia. Mr Netanyahu said the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed at Tabuk airport, and that he believed he would be taken to the United Arab Emirates. "We'll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation," Mr Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity. Asked if there was any indication of Iranian involvement, Mr Netanyahu said it was too early to say. "We'll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices, whether Iran was behind ‌it. I think we'll find out very soon," he ⁠said.

stories.title: Over 100,000 public sector workers begin work-to-rule
stories.summary: More than 100,000 public sector workers in areas such as health, education and local authorities have begun industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule. Nurses, civil servants and special needs assistants are among those taking part in the action over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said the work-to-rule means that its members in the public health service will perform only duties and responsibilities necessary for safe patient care during their rostered hours. "INMO members will not work any additional unpaid hours," the union said. "They will not attend non-clinical meetings, except where attendance is strictly necessary for direct patient care," the INMO added. The action will also involve Fórsa, the country's largest public sector union, and will see special needs assistants, health workers, civil servants and local authority employees refuse to do additional work outside of their normal duties.

stories.title: VFI say morale amongst rural publicans at rock bottom
stories.summary: Morale amongst rural publicans is at rock bottom as pubs continue to close and costs continue to rise, according to the president of the Vintners' Federation of Ireland (VFI). Members of the VFI, a body representing thousands of publicans across Ireland, gathered outside Leinster House this morning in a last-ditch plea to the Government to introduce a new tax credit to support struggling rural pubs in Budget 2027. The VFI's proposed on-trade sustainability scheme is a tax credit of €20 for every 50-litre keg of draught beer or cider sold, capped at €20,000 per pub per year. VFI President Michael O'Donovan said the tax credit would be a lifeline for pubs in rural Ireland. He said: "As we've seen over the last 20 years, pubs in rural Ireland have been disproportionately affected with costs and closures. "So today is a final plea for rural Ireland to save our pubs and to give us a tax break to try and help them survive into the future.

stories.title: Iran says it receives US response to latest proposal
stories.summary: Iran has said it had received a US response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire in the Gulf, days after President Donald ⁠Trump said he had rejected it. Iran's allies were celebrating after Washington withdrew the last of its forces from neighbouring Iraq, where 4,500 US troops died in the biggest US war of the century. More than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed in chaos unleashed after US forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003. Tehran views the pullout as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups, and a step towards its aim of driving US forces out of the region. With the US-Israeli war against Iran now entering its eighth month, Iran put forward a proposal last week under which the United States would lift its blockade of Iranian ports and Iran would reopen the disrupted Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Mr Trump said on Sunday he had rejected the proposal, although Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran had not received a formal rejection.

The Irish contingent feature among 16 declarations for Sunday’s marquee event headed by Francis-Henri Graffard’s ParisLongchamp specialist and defending champion Daryz. There will be dual Japanese representation as Admire Terra and Meisho Tabaru attempt to dethrone Daryz. Many will remember Orfevre’s agonising near-miss for Japan in 2012 before finishing second again when bumping into Treve in 2013. Leading the quest to end a losing run dating back to 1969 is Takarazuka Kinen hero Meisho Tabaru, who will be ridden by his nation’s most decorated jockey, Yutaka Take.

stories.title: Retiring Grugan happy to complete Armagh circle
stories.summary: Rory Grugan's Armagh career started 15 years ago with 70 minutes of McKenna Cup action and his manager Paddy O'Rourke using his post-match media scrum to compare him to Marty Clarke. The Down leftie was one of the hottest names in football at the time, having come so close to dragging the Mourne County to a shock All-Ireland a few months previously. As far as potential player correlations go, it seemed a heavy burden to place on the Ballymacnab youngster. Now as the All-Ireland winner tries to adapt to life without county football - something that's been present in nearly half of his 35 years on this earth - O'Rourke can take solace from being right. Grugan was a linchpin of Armagh's acceleration under Kieran McGeeney, moving from a side that yo-yoed between Division 2 and 3 to being deemed one of the best in the country over the last five years, with Celtic Cross and Ulster medals to show for it. stories.title: Former Man City chairman calls on directors to stand down
stories.summary: Manchester City's directors should step down after an independent commission found the Premier League club guilty of serious financial breaches, said former chairman David Bernstein, who described the situation as "beyond awful". On Tuesday, the Premier League said City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million (€1.05bn) over nearly a decade. The club, which denies wrongdoing, said in a statement it would appeal the ruling. "I can't think of a penalty strong enough for this, really. I mean, this is absolutely terrible. I want to raise another question, and that is the position of the board of directors," Bernstein told talkSPORT after the announcement. "Because the directors of the club, including the chief executive, who's been there for years and went through this period, are responsible for the running of the club in every respect. "And again, if this was a public company of some sort, I think the directors with something as serious as this, would have to stand down or be suspended pending the outcome of all this ... appeal or no appeal.

stories.title: Casey back, Barron and Nankivell ruled out of Bulls clash
stories.summary: Munster will welcome back Ireland internationals Craig Casey and Jeremy Loughman to the fold for this weekend's BKT United Rugby Championship clash with the Bulls, but Diarmuid Barron, Alex Nankivell, Jack O'Donoghue and Mike Haley have been ruled out. Both Casey and Loughman missed their opening round defeat to the Glasgow Warriors due to their stand down having been involved in Ireland's summer tests; but are set to return for the round two clash. New signing Jack Aungier as well as Tom Ahern, Shane Daly and Ruadhán Quinn are also primed for their season debuts on Saturday having returned to full fitness. There are injury concerns however with Mike Haley ruled out with a knee injury, while Diarmuid Barron, Alex Nankivell and Jack O'Donoghue will also miss the round two clash as they go through the return-to-play protocols. Barron's injury will be of the biggest concern to Munster, who already have Lee Barron and Max Clein out of action. New man Marnus van der Merwe is likely to start, but his back-up is still to be determined. Assistant coach Jared Payne said they will be taking a wait and see approach to the slot.

stories.title: RTÉ Supporting the Arts this October - culture on tap nationwide
stories.summary: From internationally renowned festivals and major theatrical productions to groundbreaking exhibitions and family-friendly arts experiences, October offers audiences countless opportunities to engage with the richness and diversity of Ireland's cultural life. Opera takes centre stage this month as Wexford Festival Opera, one of Ireland's most celebrated international festivals, welcomes artists and audiences from around the world to Wexford. Irish National Opera continues its nationwide programme of performances and engagement activities, while the National Concert Hall Classical Season 2026/2027 and the Wigmore Series Dublin 2026/2027 offer an outstanding programme of classical music throughout the month. Music theatre fans can enjoy The Sound of Rodgers & Hammerstein at the NCH, celebrating some of the most beloved songs from the golden age of musical theatre. Contemporary music also features strongly with Crash Ensemble's Everything is Connected, a large-scale project by composer Ed Bennett touring venues in Wexford, Kildare, Sligo, Dublin, Galway and Wicklow. Audiences can also connect with innovative cross-disciplinary work through Sounds from a Safe Harbour presents… SIRENS, an international artistic collaboration spanning Ireland and beyond. The East Cork Early Music Festival celebrates centuries of musical heritage through concerts, workshops and performances in Cork.

stories.title: Lopez sits front row for Stella McCartney's rain-soaked show
stories.summary: Jennifer Lopez sat front row for Stella McCartney’s rainy spring/summer 2027 show at Paris Fashion Week. It was apt weather for the en plein air show, which had the theme "under the sea". The 57-year-old US singer and actor arrived wearing a faux-fur shawl over the British designer’s layered Sable midi dress and a black veil, sitting with an umbrella front row. After horses trotted alongside models at McCartney’s autumn/winter show earlier this year, the lifelong animal rights campaigner turned her attention from land to sea. The collection explored marine life and the fashion industry’s relationship with animals. Ahead of the show, McCartney shared a film featuring marine biologist and oceanographer Sylvia Earle, who said the collection invited viewers "beneath the blue into a world where humans are not above nature but immersed within the systems".

stories.title: US woman on death row survives two lethal injections
stories.summary: Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Pike to death yesterday for a 1995 murder despite administering two doses of a lethal drug. Pike was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her lawyers said. "We have not been informed as to her condition," Pike's lawyers said in a statement. Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am local time yesterday for the killing she committed at the age of 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later, the US Supreme Court overturned that stay. Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers said in court filings late yesterday.

stories.title: Taxpayer loss after asylum accommodation deals ended
stories.summary: There has been a "substantial loss" to taxpayers, as a result of the termination of agreements with a number of potential asylum seeker accommodation providers. Specific figures in relation to the losses are not contained in today's report from the Comptroller and Auditor General, but there are indications that they could amount to several million euro. The C&AG says financial settlements to three parties form a "material but undisclosed part" of €35 million in accrued expenses by the Department of Justice last year, in respect of accommodation for international protection applicants. A further two prospective providers are taking legal action over the termination of agreements by the State. Chapter 14 of the report examines the cancellation of the pre-contract deals, after the Department decided to curtail the size of the international protection property portfolio and reduce it over time last year. Prior to this happening, agreements had been made with providers in respect of fifteen properties around the country.

stories.title: Burnham's big ideas ignite the Labour foot soldiers
stories.summary: He didn't say "let's rejoin the EU". He didn't even say "let's join the single market". But Andy Burnham did tell his first Labour Party Conference as UK Prime Minister that Brexit has not given Britain back control, and has done more harm than good to the UK economy. It was a speech that distilled the essence of Labour - bottled, packaged and marketed for the 21st Century. But Mr Burnham's promises on social care, housing, employment, pensions and utilities all need money. Tax money. That can only come from a growing economy. And one of the engines of growth, as Mr Burnham sees it, is the European Union - still Britain's biggest trade partner and market, but, after Brexit, not delivering what it could for British business. And if it is not delivering for business and employment, it is not delivering the taxes they yield to the government. Hence, the pressing need for a new relationship with the EU. Promising to put an end to a "decade of divisiveness and drift," Mr Burnham said: "We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market". This is what is at stake at the several-times delayed EU-UK summit that both sides say they want to happen before the end of the year. Mr Burnham and Taoiseach Micheál Martin spoke about it at their meeting in Manchester last week. Mr Martin would like it to happen during the Irish Presidency.

stories.title: Manufacturing output hits more than four year high - PMI
stories.summary: The manufacturing sector accelerated in September as production grew at its fastest pace since March 2022 and demand remained firm in domestic and overseas markets, a business survey showed today. The latest AIB Ireland Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, rose to 55.5 in September from 55.4 in August, a survey by S&P Global showed. "Output rose rapidly in September, increasing to the highest level since March 2022, with respondents citing continued robust order books," said David McNamara, AIB's chief economist. Production growth was the sharpest since March 2022, and new orders rose for a 21st month in a row. Total new work expanded at a slightly softer rate than August's 52-month high. Export orders increased, with the seasonally adjusted New Export Orders Index reaching its highest level since June. Firms cited stronger business inflows from major developed markets. Employment growth was unchanged from August's seven-month low.

stories.title: Google restricts new AI model access over safety concerns
stories.summary: Google said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers. "Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach," wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google's chief AI architect, in a blog post announcing the model. Google said it is voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and will gather feedback from testers before making it widely available. The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations. Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release. The announcement came a day after President Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including Google chief Sundar Pichai and Anthropic's Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.

stories.title: Hearn: Joshua took £10m paycut for Fury showdown
stories.summary: Anthony Joshua accepted a pay cut of over £10m (€11.7m) for his long-awaited clash with Tyson Fury to take place in the UK, according to his promoter Eddie Hearn. Joshua and Hearn held out for the fight to be staged in Britain while Saudi Arabia's boxing kingpin Turki Alalshikh, his American partner Dana White and broadcasters Netflix pressed for New York’s Madison Square Garden as the venue. Backed by the terms of their contracts with Sela, the Saudi entertainment company, they eventually got their way with the 80,000 capacity Principality Stadium chosen because of its retractable roof. But for it happen in Cardiff on 11 December, Joshua had to accept a reduced purse. Hearn said: "People started saying 'please bring the fight to the UK’ and AJ started feeling that. "To keep it in the UK he’s got to turn down eight figures plus. AJ goes to me ‘whatever you think’ and I’m like ‘no, no, no, it’s your money. I can’t make that decision for you’.
